title: A generic “preserve editorial intent” rule can backfire: prompt guardrails shifted emphasis and introduced unsupported claims
description: Adding a reusable, generic editorial-hierarchy section to the Narrative prompt did not protect the intended company-centred message. Instead, candidate runs consistently subordinated Nuëyon’s company identity and audience scope, elevated orchestration to the central positioning, and introduced unsupported validation/audience framing — causing the change to fail promotion.
audience: Prompt engineers, editorial/product teams, content ops and Narrative authors responsible for prompt design and content safety
rationale: Teams often add high-level guardrails to prevent drift. This experiment shows a plausible, concrete risk: a broadly-worded editorial rule can change emphasis and add unsupported claims rather than preserve intent. That lesson matters because it affects whether prompt edits can be safely rolled into production without introducing factual or editorial regressions.
evidence: Candidate prompt added a generic “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” section. Candidate Narrative mean score fell to 4.00/10 (baseline 6.00/10); candidate Compose mean 3.33/10 (baseline 5.67/10). All three candidate Narrative runs and all three candidate Compose runs made orchestration central (failed gate C) and introduced unsupported additions (failed hard gate D in every candidate run). The experiment decision: “Do not promote.” The production prompt was restored byte-for-byte.

title: A reproducible, gate-driven rubric for safe prompt changes — and why hard gates matter
description: The experiment documents a controlled, auditable process for evaluating prompt edits: baseline reuse, three-run comparison, explicit scoring rubric with a hard factual-restraint gate, SHA-256 prompt/input hashes, and a byte-for-byte rollback. The process led to a clear do-not-promote decision when the candidate failed critical gates.
audience: ML governance, research/experimentation teams, MLops and product teams who approve prompt or model prompt changes
rationale: Concrete, repeatable evaluation criteria and binary promotion gates (especially hard gates for factual/editorial restraint) make prompt-change decisions defensible and reduce the risk of shipping regressions. This experiment is a practical example of that governance in action.
evidence: The report records baseline and candidate runs (three each), an explicit 0–2 scoring rubric across A–E with D as a hard promotion gate, SHA-256 hashes for prompts and inputs, saved diffs, full console logs and outputs, and an explicit rollback verifying the original prompt SHA matched the frozen baseline. The decision section: candidate was worse on mean score, failed key gates, and was not promoted.

title: Internal contradictions in a Synthesis can make editorial intent fragile
description: The baseline Synthesis paired a company-first emphasis with a later statement that called orchestration “central to the product direction.” That internal tension—explicitly noted in the report—likely made the editorial hierarchy fragile and easier for the candidate prompt change to tip toward a technical framing.
audience: Editors, narrative designers, product communicators, and prompt writers who author or curate source Synthesis content
rationale: If the source material contains mixed signals about primary emphasis, attempts to externally enforce hierarchy (via prompts) are less likely to succeed. Clearing contradictions in the Synthesis itself may be a necessary precursor to reliable editorial-preservation rules.
evidence: The report states: “The baseline Synthesis pairs company identity with Compose in its top-level emphasis, but also contains a later description calling orchestration ‘central to the product direction.’ That internal tension may have reinforced the technical angle.” Candidate runs then consistently made orchestration central rather than preserving the company-first audience emphasis.

title: Narrowing variance isn’t always improvement: a prompt edit can stabilize outputs around the wrong behavior
description: The candidate prompt change produced more consistent outputs (very low run-to-run variance) but consistently reproduced the wrong editorial outcome. Reducing variability therefore masked a persistent failure mode instead of improving fidelity.
audience: Experiment designers, prompt engineers, ML researchers tracking model variability and stability
rationale: Experimenters often treat reduced variance as progress. This case shows a different outcome: the candidate produced a stable but incorrect behaviour (subordinated company identity, centralized orchestration). Recognizing this helps teams prefer qualitative gate checks over raw consistency metrics.
evidence: Narrative candidate runs had mean 4.00/10 with sample SD 0.00 (baseline SD 1.00). Compose candidate runs showed reduced variability (candidate SD 0.58 vs baseline SD 1.53) yet preserved the same editorial regressions (orchestration centrality and unsupported additions). The report notes the change narrowed variability but resulted in a stable failure.
